findings.element: The received chain: unfurl to loading to the plan (states unfurl, loading, phone, desk, day)
findings.problem: The whole product contains one moment of motion - transition: top var(--t-slow) on .b-item when a row is moved - and it lives inside the owner's editor, which the audience never opens. There are zero @keyframes in b.css and no .animate() anywhere in render-b.js. So the screen the brief says the company is judged by opens fully formed, at rest, identical to a screenshot: the unfurl card, the 79, the rail and the first mark all arrive already there. Having driven all thirteen states, I can name a memorable IDEA (distance drawn as distance) but not a memorable MOMENT. Linear, Stripe and Vercel all buy their emotional credit at exactly this instant, and here it is spent on nothing. The restraint elsewhere is real and mostly right; total absence is not restraint, it is an unmade decision.
findings.fix: Give the received view exactly one arrival, on first paint only. In b.css add @keyframes b-draw { from { transform: scaleY(0); } to { transform: scaleY(1); } } and apply it to the measure's rail with transform-origin: top; animation: b-draw var(--t-slow) var(--ease) both. Stagger the marks and their words with animation: b-rise var(--t-base) var(--ease) both; animation-delay: calc(var(--i) * 60ms), where --i is the row index already available at render and b-rise runs opacity 0 / translateY(4px) to rest. Cap the total at 600ms. Put the whole block inside the existing prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference guard so the reduced-motion assertion keeps holding, and gate it on a data-arrived attribute set once so no repaint ever replays it.

findings.element: state=day, .b-dayNote (render-b.js:1552) and the pinned block above it
findings.problem: The morning is the emotional apex and the one place the product's own instrument should pay out. For months the audience watches a number fall - 79, 40, 3 - and on the day it becomes the word 'Today', which is a genuinely good move. Then the single line beneath it is 'This is the day the plan was for.': flat, backward-facing, stating what the reader already knows and measuring nothing. Meanwhile the number that would actually land is already computed and already on the page - expand BEHIND YOU and the ninth row down reads '274 days back / We said yes / Fri 2 Jan'. The distance travelled, the whole point of an instrument that measures distance, is buried behind a disclosure at the foot of the morning screen while the hero line is filler.
findings.fix: Replace the string at render-b.js:1552 with the span, derived from the same accessor that writes the past rail's 'days back': h("p.b-dayNote", { text: fmt.dayCount(days(firstCoveredMilestone.date, TODAY)) + " since " + firstCoveredMilestone.title.toLowerCase() + "." }), which on this fixture renders '274 days since we said yes.' Keep it in the same .b-dayNote register and position so the composition is unchanged. If the plan holds no covered moment, fall back to the current sentence.

findings.element: .b-behindRow and .b-behindDate:empty { display: none; } (b.css:474), the BEHIND YOU disclosure, states owner-flight / phone / desk
findings.problem: Open the past on any screen state and the couple's own words land on two different left edges inside one four-row block: 'We said yes' and 'The Orchard reserved' start at x=132 (390px) / x=699 (1440px), while 'City hotel shortlist' starts at x=20 / x=587 because the cancelled row has no date and the empty lane is collapsed. The block reads as a ragged accident at exactly the moment the reader is looking at the most personal content in the product. The master already judges this defect correctly on paper - the comment at b.css:1209 says a wrapping flex row 'put its three rows on three different left edges' and restacks the print row to fix it - and then concludes 'on screen the row stays as it is, where it is correct.' By the file's own standard it is not correct.
findings.fix: Stop collapsing the lane; let the status label wrap instead. Delete .b-behindDate:empty { display: none; } at b.css:474 so the empty date lane keeps its 96px and every title starts on one edge. Then change .b-behindState from flex: none to flex: 0 1 auto with min-width: 0 (keeping margin-left: auto), so that when title plus label exceed the row at 390px the label drops onto its own line under the title rather than starving it - the row is already flex-wrap: wrap. Leave the .b-print overrides at b.css:1210-1212 untouched.

findings.problem: Four filled rectangles at rgba(255,255,255,0.1) with 4px radii - 107x86, 227x26, 188x23, 92x15. They are the only filled slabs in a system otherwise built entirely from hairlines, type weight and one indigo dot, and they are the first thing the audience ever sees. On the stalled path they stare at them for seconds. Nothing in the finished plan is a rounded grey block, so the loading frame does not look like this product; it looks like a generic skeleton borrowed from elsewhere and dropped into a Swiss composition. The gate proves the reserve is honest and sized to the real geometry; it cannot see that it is drawn in the wrong vocabulary.
findings.fix: Redraw the reserve in the system's own marks. On .b-skel replace background with background: none; border-radius: 0; border-bottom: 1px solid var(--fore-12), so each reserved line becomes a rule of the exact width sitting on the baseline the real string will occupy. Give the numeral's reserve border: 1px solid var(--fore-12); border-radius: 0 instead, so it reads as an outlined slot for the figure rather than a slab. Keep every measured width and height exactly as they are so the reserve floor and 'invents no measure' assertions hold unchanged.

findings.element: .b-stick micro-label 'TODAY IS 16 JULY' with the scroll readout beneath it, states owner-flight / desk at >=1024
findings.problem: The pinned column is the best interaction in the master - scroll and the line under the rule becomes '22 August - 37 days away', naming where the eye is standing. Driven, it also breaks its own grammar. At rest the block reads 'TODAY IS 16 JULY / Nothing is planned until 1 August.', where the sentence is a consequence of the label. Scrolled, it reads 'TODAY IS 16 JULY / 5 September - 51 days away', where the label announces one date and the line under it states a different one. In the most-looked-at block on the owner's screen, the section head stops describing its own content, which is the one thing a section head must never do.
findings.fix: Keep both statements of today and separate the registers. In render-b.js, when the readout is showing a scrolled position rather than the rest sentence, insert a second micro-label above the value using the existing micro() helper so the block reads 'TODAY IS 16 JULY' / 'IN VIEW' / '5 September - 51 days away', set at var(--fore-62) like the label beside it; swap it back out when the readout returns to the rest sentence. This adds one label line and removes nothing, so neither statement of today is lost.

biggestWin: The measure itself: distance drawn as distance. A fourteen-day gap is visibly twice a seven-day gap, the count travels with the words it names while the tick stays on the true pixel, and one indigo dot marks the only thing that is next. Driven rather than read it gets better - the pinned column's readout renames itself as you scroll ('22 August - 37 days away'), so the masthead always tells you where on the plan your eye is standing, and the empty left column turns out to be the reserved room the editor opens into. On paper the same idea becomes the strongest object in the deck: the A4 keepsake is genuinely award-standard work, and 'One of them did not happen.' beneath a struck-through line is the most honest sentence in the product. Palette discipline is total, the keyboard model is eleven clean stops with no dead controls, and the publish copy ('It carries the day, the distance and the plan, and nothing else: no notes, no suppliers, no prices.') earns trust in a single line. A discerning stranger would believe a top studio made this and would pay for it. What keeps it off 9.5 is not craft, it is payload: the audience's entire experience is a beautifully set static document, and at both emotional peaks - the arrival of the link and the morning itself - the product declines to spend the instrument it spent months building. That is one small build and four pieces of polish, not a different decision.
